title: Three Reasons You Shouldn't Use Your Browser's Password Manager (and What to Use Instead)
body:
Built-in tools have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality.
            
                        
    
                    
        
        
        
    
                                Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                            
        
        
        September 4, 2026
            
            
                        Credit:  Ian Moore/Lifehacker/Getty Images
                            
    
        
        Most modern browsers have built-in password management, allowing you to save your credentials and automatically fill them when logging into your accounts on various websites. And while Google Password Manager on Chrome and similar tools in other browsers like Firefox, Brave, and Microsoft Edge certainly simplify the process of storing and using stronger passwords, they have major limitations when it comes to security and functionality. Here's why you should use a dedicated password manager instead.Browser password managers only work within the browserIf you store your passwords in your browser, it can fill your credentials on websites within the browser itself. (If you're an Android user, Google Password Manager also syncs to your device and works across any browser or app.) But if you use multiple browsers or want to log into apps on your iPhone or PC, you'll have to manually copy and paste your password from the browser into those form fields—not ideal, from a standpoint of both convenience and security. Browser password managers are more vulnerable to security risksBrowser password management is, on a basic level, secure: Google uses the same AES encryption in transit and at rest that many dedicated password managers do, and allows it you to add biometric authentication for auto-filling credentials. However, they're not zero-knowledge by default: Google manages your encryption key unless you enable on-device encryption so that your vault can only be unlocked on your device, by you, with your Google password or biometrics. Firefox also uses AES-256 encryption and has a "primary password" feature to protect your stored data, without which anyone who has access to your computer or browser profile can view your saved passwords. It's on the user to add these layers of security, as they're not on by default.As Wired points out, the more serious problem isn't encryption, but rather the risk inherent in storing passwords in a high-value account that could be targeted—either by someone who gains access to your device or as part of a takeover attempt, such as a phishing or credential stuffing attack. This creates a single point of failure, and if someone gets into your Google account or your browser of choice, your passwords for everything else are also compromised. Browser password managers have only basic featuresBrowser password managers do basically one thing, which is store your login credentials and fill them in on websites when you visit them in the browser. Google Password Manager will also alert you if your password has been compromised in a breach, but most browsers lack any additional tools and features, such as password customization, secure sharing, email masking, emergency access, and storage for payment cards, identity data, and documents. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Use a dedicated third-party password manager insteadThe solution is to opt for a dedicated password manager that works across platforms and devices and offers a layer of protection outside of your browser. There are many excellent password managers to choose from, including free services like Bitwarden and privacy-focused Proton Pass (which also has a decent free tier). The best password managers also have features like secure file storage, encrypted credential sharing, and data breach monitoring, making them useful tools in your privacy and security arsenal. Of course, even a browser password manager is better than nothing at all, if the alternative is to reuse the same easy-to-remember credentials across your accounts. (It's also likely your reused passwords don't meet basic security standards and can be easily guessed.) Password storage in Chrome, Firefox, and other browsers do reduce the friction of shifting to strong, unique passwords for your accounts, and that alone is a solid step. But a third-party password manager is a superior choice if you're willing to invest a bit of time and energy into setting it up. 
            
                        
                
                    
                                            
                
                
                                            
    More by Emily

title: Firefox Can Now Block Ads on iOS (but You Have to Enable It)
body:
Emily Long
                            
        
            Emily Long
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceEmily Long is a freelance writer based in Salt Lake City. After graduating from Duke University, she spent several years reporting on the federal workforce for Government Executive, a publication of Atlantic Media Company, in Washington, D.C. She has nearly a decade of experience as a freelancer covering tech (including issues related to security, privacy, and streaming) as well as personal finance and travel. In addition to Lifehacker, her work has been featured on Wirecutter, Tom’s Guide, and ZDNET. Emily has also worked as a travel guide around the U.S. and as a content editor. She has a masters in social work and is a licensed therapist in Utah.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 1, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Kenneth Cheung / iStock Unreleased via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device, as Mozilla is officially rolling out native ad blocking.
                                            Most ads will be blocked, but users will still see search engine ads and sponsored content from Firefox.
                                            The feature is off by default, so you need to enable it yourself if you want to use it.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Firefox users on iOS can now get rid of a lot of ad noise when browsing on their mobile device. Following a slow "experimental" period, Mozilla is now officially rolling out native ad blocking, which you can enable once the tool is available in your app. According to Mozilla's support page detailing the new feature, Firefox's new feature can block third-party ad networks and exchanges along with many third-party ads served on websites at the network level. It can also block ad-related trackers, pop-ups, and overlays. The platform is still letting some ads through, though: For example, you'll still see ads in search results from engines like Google, Bing, and DuckDuckGo, as well as sponsored content on the Firefox Home and New Tab pages. There may also be ads that aren't covered by the EasyList filter list. Of course, Firefox isn't the only browser to natively block ads on iOS. For example, both DuckDuckGo and Brave have built-in ad blocking in their mobile apps and also allow you to disable their own search ads. Note that ad-blocking functionality doesn't extend outside of the Firefox iOS app, but URL filters in iOS 26, along with a third-party app like Wipr 2, can block ads in other apps. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Ad blocking in Firefox will be off by default. To enable it, open the iOS app, tap the three dots, and go to Settings > Browsing. Under the Content header, toggle on Ad Blocker. You can do this from the Site menu by tapping Ad Blocker (underneath the site name and URL), which will open the Browsing menu directly. The site menu will show you at a glance whether ad blocking is on or off.

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple says the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max feature the best battery life on iPhones to date.
                                            There's a new 5-minute fast wired charging feature which offers 50% battery life for just 15 minutes of charging time.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        While the iPhone 18 Pro looks similar to last year's model, the internals are a different story. The new A20 Pro processor with 32 Neural Engine cores will go a long way helping with on-device AI tasks—but you might not feel those differences all the time.The new updates to battery life and charging, however, will make an actual difference in daily use on the iPhone 18 Pro and iPhone 18 Pro Max. Apple is promising the best battery life on an iPhone yet, and is finally supporting faster wired charging.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Apple
                    
    
According to Apple, the regular sized iPhone 18 Pro will have the same battery life as the outgoing, larger iPhone 17 Pro Max model, which is quite a big deal. Apple is combining the efficiency gains in the A20 Pro chip with new battery technology to deliver this large leap in battery life. 
You will get 45 hours of video playback on the iPhone 18 Pro Max, and 36 hours on the iPhone 18 Pro model. The iPhone 18 Pro will last 24 hours per charge, while the 18 Pro Max can go up to 30 hours.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
According to Apple, this is based on tests performed with Apple's 40W Dynamic Power Adapter with a 60W max charging speed. Wired fast charging is also supported with 60W-capable USB-C cables and USB PD 3.1 adapters that support Adjustable Voltage Supply.Faster wired charging finally comes to the iPhoneThe world of Android flagships is filled with quick-charging smartphones, and some of that clout will now come over to the iPhone as well. A quick five-minute wired charge will give you up to six hours of video playback, and more importantly, you get 50% charging in just 15 minutes. Even wireless charging is faster, with 50% charging in around 30 minutes.

title: Apple's 'Reference Image' Preserves Your Original Photos (Even After You Edit Them)
description: Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple int
body:
Figuring out what’s real online is only getting harder, and AI watermarks can only go so far to identify fakes. But today, Apple introduced a new standard to at least help identify real images taken directly on an iPhone: Apple Reference Image. It won’t solve the problem of finding the truth online, but it could be a helpful tool towards that goal.The new feature will be available on iPhone 18 Pro models to start. It works by taking signed sensor data from the camera and using it to create a reference picture that can’t be edited, alongside a version that can be changed. The idea here is to give you a version of the picture that’s authenticated at the moment of capture, which you can compare against any modified versions later.
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Credit: Apple
                    
    
This provenance metadata can be preserved through certain supported sharing methods, which for now means select other Apple devices can check their verification status. That doesn’t mean that anyone can check the veracity of an image—especially if the version that gets posted and shared is an edited variant—but it provides a tool for the person or organization that took the picture originally to offer proof of verification.
This tool comes alongside the announcement that Apple will soon add support for the SynthID standard. This will potentially help users identify when an image has been created or modified with AI. Apple joins a long (though not exactly comprehensive) list of major tech companies to support the standard, including OpenAI, Nvidia, and obviously Google, the original creator of SynthID.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
We’re still in the midst of a scattershot image verification ecosystem. Apple’s Reference Image is a clever implementation that gives the end user a signed original to compare a picture against, which is a step up from C2PA metadata that merely embeds information about an image’s origin. It’s still unclear how widely these verification tools will be implemented and how easy it will be for users to trace where an image comes from and how, precisely, it was modified, but still, something is better than nothing.

title: Microsoft Outlook Is Down
body:
Jake Peterson
                            
        
            Jake Peterson
                
                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        August 31, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Thomas Fuller/SOPA Images/LightRocket via Getty Images
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Microsoft Outlook is down for many users as of Monday afternoon.
                                            Downdetector highlights tens of thousands of users reports suggesting issues with Outlook.
                                            In addition, other Microsoft services, including Microsoft 365, are also down.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you're trying to check your inbox or send an email in Microsoft Outlook, only to find the app uncooperative, you're not alone. Outlook is currently down for many users as of Monday afternoon. That's apparent to anyone who can't get the app to work: Downdetector, which highlights user reports for app outages, shows tens of thousands of reports as of 3:00 p.m. ET, and while the rate of reports does seem to be decreasing, thousands of reports keep coming in with every refresh.  As CNET reports, Microsoft has officially confirmed the outage itself. The company posted on its Microsoft 365 Status X account, stating: “We’ve identified an issue with an authentication component which is contributing to impact. To address this, we’ve developed a remediation strategy, and we’re applying it to a portion of infrastructure to test its efficacy. Once we’ve confirmed this resolves impact, we’ll apply the solution more broadly. For more information, please see EX1464935 in the admin center.”As such, the company should be rolling out a fix in due time, though it's difficult to say how long that may be. Recent outages have been fixed in a matter of hours, while others have stretched into the following day. At the time of writing, Downdetector shows that 38% of users are reporting issues receiving messages in Outlook, while 24% report issues with the app, and 21% with logging in. 
As it happens, Outlook isn't the only Microsoft product facing issues: Users report that Microsoft Teams, Microsoft Store, Microsoft Azur  and Microsoft 365 in general are experiencing  issues. In addition, OpenAI users are reporting issues with ChatGPT. 
            
                What do you think so far?

body:
Khamosh Pathak
                            
        
            Khamosh Pathak
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperienceKhamosh Pathak is a freelance tech journalist with over 13 years of experience writing online. An accounting graduate, he turned his interest in writing and technology into a career. He holds a specialization in user experience design from ISDI Parsons in Mumbai, where he sought to deepen his understanding of UX, consumer devices, and interplay between software and technology.Khamosh has written thousands of how-tos and guides on every major platform (iOS, macOS, Android, and Windows). He got started writing how-tos and guides for Guiding Tech, where he also published several e-books. His work has also been seen at MakeUseOf, How-To Geek, and PCMag. He is truly passionate about brewing good coffee.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            Apple is increasing the price of all existing iPhone models, including iPhone 17e, iPhone 16, and iPhone 17.
                                            The newly released AirPods 5 are actually cheaper than the outgoing model.
                                            The Apple Watch series has surprisingly missed the price bump.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        RAMageddon is real, and it’s finally come for the iPhone. Thanks to the ever-increasing costs of memory and storage, the prices of virtually all tech products are going up. A couple of months ago, Apple increased the pricing for the Mac and the iPad, by a couple of hundred dollars. Now, it’s the iPhone’s turn: Suddenly, all the iPhones are now $100 more expensive than they were yesterday, and the newly announced models are $100 more expensive than last year. But it’s not all doom and gloom. The new AirPods are actually cheaper, and mercifully, some Apple products remain the same price.The $100 iPhone bump
    
            
            
                                        Credit: Khamosh Pathak
                    
    
At the September keynote event, Apple introduced the iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max. The 18 Pro starts at $1,199 for 256GB storage, and the iPhone 18 Pro Max is now $1,399. Both of them are $100 more than the starting price of comparable iPhone 17 Pro/Max models.
The price bump doesn't stop with the new phones: Apple has flipped a switch and bumped prices on all existing iPhone models by $100. While Apple did not introduce an iPhone 18, the price of the iPhone 17 has quietly gone up; it now starts at $899 for the 256GB model instead of $799. The older iPhone 16 model is now $799, while the "budget" iPhone 17e now sells for $699. Even the iPhone Air has gone up to $1099.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
Apple Watch pricing stays the sameSurprisingly, the RAM and storage costs haven’t hit the Apple Watch yet, or, at least, Apple is willing to absorb those increases for these smaller devices. The Series 12 Apple Watch with a new S11 processor and on-device Apple Intelligence features starts at the same $399 price as the Apple Watch 11. The new Apple Watch Ultra 4 also remains at the same $799 introductory price as the Ultra 3.AirPods are now cheaper (and better) than everOne popular product escaped the price bump: I was surprised to see a new standard AirPods model at the iPhone 18 Pro keynote, but the price drop was even more unexpected. The base AirPods 5 now come with built-in ANC (which used to cost extra), along with better transparency and improved sound features, and they are just $129, the cost of the outgoing AirPods 4 without ANC. Apple does have a more expensive model of AirPods 5 that comes with a wireless charging case, better battery life, and an on-stem voice control feature for $149, or $30 cheaper than the outgoing AirPods 4 with ANC model.

She has been writing professionally since 2018, creating product reviews, affiliate articles, and search ads for global clients while working with Rubix Agency and Cognizant. Previously, she spent a year teaching English at the junior high level.An avid reader since childhood, Pradershika's idea of extreme sports is staying up to read “just one more chapter.” She lives in India.

    Table of Contents
    
        
        The Linksys RE7000 Range Booster is designed to fill weak-signal gaps without changing your existing router, and it's currently on sale for just $27.99 as an open-box unit on StackSocial. Open box usually means the packaging has been handled or returned, but the unit itself has been checked and works like new. This model plugs straight into a wall outlet and keeps the top socket usable, so it doesn’t block access in tight spaces. In a typical home, Linksys claims coverage up to 2,500 square feet, though real-world results depend on walls and layout.Setup is simple: You press the WPS button to sync it with your router and use a phone or laptop to finish the process in a few minutes. It works with most routers, including those provided by internet service providers. Once it's in place, the extender works by pulling in your existing Wi-Fi signal and pushing it further into areas that struggle to stay connected. It supports AC1900 speeds across dual bands, which is enough for everyday use like streaming, browsing, or video calls, assuming your base connection is strong enough. MU-MIMO support helps when several people are connected at once, so one person streaming a show does not slow down someone else on a video call.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
There is also seamless roaming, which keeps your phone connected to the strongest signal automatically as you move around the house. The included Gigabit Ethernet port is also useful if you want a more stable wired connection for a console or desktop in a weak-signal area. That said, there are limits to what an extender like this can do—this is a Wi-Fi 5 extender, so it will not match the speeds or efficiency of newer Wi-Fi 6 or 7 hardware. But for $28, this Wi-Fi extender is a great deal for fixing dead zones in your house.

title: This Is the Best Preorder Deal for 'The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time' on the Nintendo Switch 2
body:
Daniel Oropeza
                            
        
            Daniel Oropeza
                
                                            Shopping Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceDaniel is Lifehacker's Shopping Editor covering tech deals and reviewing TVs, headphones, speakers, and projectors. He earned his master’s in journalism from Columbia University and has reported for the Miami Herald. He lives in Atlanta.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise

        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
            Deal pricing and availability subject to change after time of publication.
    
            Credit: Rene Ramos
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Nintendo announced the new The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time at its Nintendo Direct event this week. And already, Walmart has the game available for $59.99 (originally $69.99) for pre-order. Judging by how fast other pre-orders for the new remake have been going since the announcement, I wouldn't be surprised if this pre-order deal sells out too. And you're unlikely to see another discount on this major Nintendo game like the one Walmart is offering.
The Nintendo Switch 2 The Legend of Zelda 40th Anniversary Edition console does not come with the game, so you will have to buy a physical or digital copy separately. Nintendo announced that the first printing of physical copies would include a "textured foil cover art" while supplies last, but it's unclear whether this sale is for that version. No pre-order product page lists whether it's a foil version, but as long as you're pre-ordering, you improve your chances of being in that pool.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
The game will release on Nov. 5, and it's a faithful remake of the original The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time with improved graphics, cutscenes with dialogue, new mechanics (Link can jump now), and other new additions. It would be inaccurate to call it a one-to-one remake. I'm hoping Nintendo finally gives us the Light Temple that the original game on the N64 could not fit in the game. We'll just have to find out on Nov. 5, when the game releases.

        At $154.99 for the Wi-Fi model, Apple’s refurbished 9th-generation iPad lands in the same price range as many budget Android tablets while still offering the polished experience people usually expect from an iPad. The Wi-Fi + Cellular version is probably the better value here since it costs only $15 more—and having built-in cellular connectivity means you are not constantly depending on public Wi-Fi or tethering from your phone, which makes a noticeable difference for commuters, students, rideshare drivers, and frequent travelers.And since Apple still supports this model with iPadOS 26 updates, you're not immediately stepping into outdated software either. That, combined with the “Grade A” refurbished condition (comes with little to no cosmetic wear) and included one-year warranty, still makes this older iPad a reasonable option for students, parents, travelers, or anyone looking for a dependable secondary device for reading, streaming, video calls, light work, and casual gaming. That said, it is not built for demanding creative workloads like professional video editing or heavy multitasking, but that limitation feels reasonable considering the price. The biggest compromise is the 64GB storage capacity, which works best for people who mostly stream content rather than store large games or video files locally.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
And while its A13 Bionic chip is older by Apple standards, it still keeps up with everyday use—apps launch quickly, Safari browsing stays smooth with multiple tabs open, and streaming services run without feeling sluggish. The 10.2-inch Retina display also holds up surprisingly well for everyday use, especially for reading articles and ebooks or watching videos. You still get Touch ID in the home button, stereo speakers, and support for the first-generation Apple Pencil for handwritten notes or sketching. Battery life also remains practical, with Apple estimating up to 10 hours of use on a charge, which is enough for a full day of browsing, streaming, and light work. All things considered, this 9th-gen iPad is a great deal.

title: All the Differences Between the AirPods 5, AirPods 4, and AirPods Pro 3
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    We may earn a commission from links on this page.
    
            Credit: Apple
                            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        I've been rocking the first-gen AirPods Pro since 2021, so you can safely say that I take my time with gadget upgrades. But I was so shocked to see Apple's new AirPods 5 are cheaper and better than the AirPods 4 that I initially thought I might've just found the easier upgrade decision of all time. But then, my sense of propriety kicked in: Experience has taught me to weigh my options carefully before buying anything, so I decided to compare (on paper, at least) the AirPods 5 with their counterparts from Apple: the AirPods 4 with active noise cancellation (ANC) and the AirPods Pro 3. Here's what I found.AirPods Pro 3 still offer the best noise cancellationAs much as I want to love the AirPods 5, and as much as I appreciate the fact that ANC is now standard on all Apple earbuds, the new model's noise cancellation feature is significantly weaker than that on the AirPods Pro 3. According to the specs comparison on Apple's website, the AirPods Pro 3 has "3x more Active Noise Cancellation (ANC) than AirPods 5." This is the most important AirPods feature for me, and I'm seriously considering paying that $120 premium (at retail) for better ANC. Having said that, the AirPods 5 do get "1.5x more ANC than AirPods 4 (with ANC)," so it could be a good upgrade for many people. AirPods 5 have the worst battery life (but it's probably good enough)According to Apple, the AirPods 5 offer up to five hours of battery on a single charge (with ANC on), and 22 hours of battery life if you include the power from the charging case. If you get the cheapest variant of the AirPods 5 (without wireless charging), these numbers drop to four hours on one charge, and 20 hours from the charging case. This is lower than the AirPods 4 (with ANC), which offer 5 hours of battery life and 30 hours including the charging case. The AirPods Pro 3 have the best battery life, with 8 hours of playback time on a single charge and 24 hours with the charging case.
If you opt for the $149 variant of the AirPods 5, you're getting improved battery life, on-stem volume controls, a wireless charging case, and a speaker for Find My. I think those features are easily worth the extra $20 over the base variant of the AirPods 5. I think the extra hour of battery life is an essential feature, and all the others are great quality-of-life additions. It's nice to control volume by swiping the stem of the AirPods, and after switching to wireless charging last year, I can't see myself going back. The case's speaker, which plays a sound and allows you to locate it when it disappears into your couch, might be worth the cost all on its own.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
AirPods 5's fit may be better for some peopleThe AirPods Pro 3's ear tips rest in your ear canal. This is optimal for ensuring the best noise cancellation and a secure fit, but it doesn't work for everyone. I know quite a few people who prefer the AirPods 4's design, where the earbuds rest outside the ear canal. The AirPods 5 follow the same design language and may be the better choice for some people. You can't use the AirPods 5 as a hearing aidYou can use your AirPods Pro 3 as a temporary hearing aid, but that doesn't extend to the AirPods 5 or the AirPods 4. If you need Apple's hearing health features, you should choose the AirPods Pro 3, which have been cleared by the FDA for use as a hearing-aid.

title: Why the iPhone 18 Pro's Variable Aperture Is a Big Development for Smartphone Photography
body:
Pranay Parab
                            
        
            Pranay Parab
                
                                                                        Freelance Writer
                                                            
            
            
        
            ExperiencePranay Parab is an independent tech journalist based in Mumbai, India. He covers tech for Lifehacker, and specializes in tutorials and in-depth features.
        
        
            Areas of Expertise
        
        Read Full Bio
    

    
                                        
        
        
        September 9, 2026
                
        Add as a preferred source on Google

    
    
        Add as a preferred source on Google

            Credit: Apple
                            
            
                Key Takeaways
                                            The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max have a variable-aperture lens.
                                            The variable aperture lens is unavailable on the more expensive iPhone Duo.
                                            Variable aperture gives you more control over photo lighting.
                                            Aperture values range from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0m.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        Every year, Apple claims its newly launched iPhones have the best cameras ever, and those improvements usually revolve around improved sensors, lenses, and software updates. This year, though, there's an unusual camera upgrade that's going to make a massive difference to your photos and videos: The iPhone 18 Pro and the iPhone 18 Pro Max have a variable-aperture lens, a feature unavailable on the much more expensive iPhone Duo. Variable aperture gives you far greater control over lighting in your iPhone photos.What does "camera aperture" mean?A camera's aperture lets you control how much light reaches the lens. For a brighter photo, you want to let in more light; for a darker one, you'd ideally let in less. This system is similar to the pupils of your eyes, which constrict when the light is too bright and dilate when you suddenly go from bright sunshine to a dark room. In DSLR cameras, you can see overlapping blades that partially cover the lens. This opening increases or decreases in size depending on the aperture value. This technology is expensive to implement in a smartphone lens, and so far, the improvement in photos hasn't been good enough to justify the investment. That's why it's rare to find the feature in most phones. Apple added variable aperture to its smartphones for the first time with the launch of the iPhone 18 Pro series. (Note that aperture values are denoted in f-numbers, which means that when you adjust a camera's aperture, the value looks something like f/1.8, f/4.0, etc. The lower the f-number, the brighter the image becomes.)
How variable aperture changes photos and videosThe iPhone 18 Pro has three rear cameras, but only the main camera offers a variable aperture. It's a 48-megapixel sensor with four aperture f-numbers supported. You can pick an aperture value from f/1.48, f/1.8, f/2.8, and f/4.0m, which should make it significantly easier to get the exposure just right in difficult lighting conditions. You'll also be able to take better photos in low light and try a few additional creative shots with your iPhone 18 Pro. Having a variable aperture is great for controlling depth of field, so you can easily blur the background or keep it in sharp focus when you take photos.
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
With a larger aperture (f/1.48), you'll be able to reduce the depth of field and blur the background for shots that require focus on a single subject. You can use a smaller aperture (f/4.0) to capture stunning landscapes, where you want the entire photo to be in focus. If you're thinking that your iPhone already does these things, you're sort of right. But it's worth remembering that up until now, iPhones had to rely on software to perform these tasks, which gets the job done, but the results aren't always exactly what you'd visualize. Having hardware control over aperture gives you greater control over the output and brings the final result much closer to what you visualized. In theory, variable aperture should make the iPhone 18 Pro better for astrophotography, too, but until all of these tasks are tested, it's hard to say how much impact the new feature will have.

title: A Bunch of AI Platforms Are Down, Including ChatGPT
body:
Jake Peterson

                                            Senior Technology Editor
                                    
            
            
        
            ExperienceJake Peterson is Lifehacker’s Tech Editor, and has been covering tech news and how-tos for nearly a decade. His team covers all things technology, including AI, smartphones, computers, game consoles, and subscriptions.

                Key Takeaways
                                            ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok are all experiencing downtime Thursday morning.
                                            OpenAI, Anthropic, and SpaceX AI all confirm issues with their platforms.
                                            It's not clear what the root cause of the issue is at this time, or whether the outages are related.
                                    
            
    Table of Contents
    
        
        If you had trouble accessing AI platforms Thursday morning, you're not alone. Apps and services, including ChatGPT, Claude, and Grok, were down, or experienced issues with service. ChatGPT and Grok were both unresponsive when I tried to use them, while Claude appeared to respond, at least for me. ChatGPT appears to be experiencing the most issues, at least per Downdetector. The site, which accepts user reports of issues with apps and services, currently shows tens of thousands of reports for ChatGPT alone. Claude and Grok had fewer reports, but still many (thousands) over the course of this morning. According to OpenAI's status page, the company had experienced issues with both ChatGPT and Codex. Anthropic had also acknowledged issues with Claude, including for its Mythos 5.1, Fable 5.1, and Opus 5 models, and said it is working on a fix. SpaceXAI shows that all Grok functions appear to be down at this time. As of 1:19 p.m. ET, all three services now report that they're now up and running. 
            
                What do you think so far?
            
        
It's not clear exactly what caused these issues, or if they were all related to one another. Typically, outages like these are solved relatively quickly, so it's not a surprise that all three were able to get their systems back by early afternoon. I'll continue to monitor the situation and update this piece accordingly.
